dimensions.name: Reference mining & contract inference

evidence.note: Reads both fixture next-shims.d.ts files (app-basic and pages-basic) — grounds the next/* contract in the fixtures' declared type signatures.

Greps all next/* imports/requires across both fixture apps and writes a consolidated inventory to /tmp/nextimports.txt; inspects route file layouts. Systematic mining of fixture-side contracts, more than a skim.
Greps e2e specs for expect/toHaveText/status assertions and reads fixtures/helpers to infer behavioral contracts from tests rather than pure guessing.

Plans and begins the implementation (Vite SSR middleware, esbuild transpile, custom shims) with NO consultation of the vendored Vite plugin API or Next source — plugin lifecycle and framework semantics assumed from memory.
Trajectory collapses into endless npm-install / dev-server terminal recovery; no further reference reading or re-consultation of source to resolve ambiguous semantics ever occurs.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent genuinely mined the fixture type shims and next/* usage (both shim files read, all imports grepped into an inventory, test expectations scanned), grounding next/* contracts in actual signatures — above the level-3 'skims one or two, proceeds on assumption.' But it never once opened the vendored Vite or Next.js source and approached the Vite plugin lifecycle and framework semantics from memory, so it does not meet level 5's 'reads the relevant Vite plugin API surface,' and there is no re-consultation of source under ambiguity (level 8). This places it at 4: solid fixture-contract inference, zero vendored-source engagement.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Early 'Plan:' prose is tactical exploration (list contents, inspect shims/tests) rather than a decomposition of the framework into ordered, independently-verifiable subsystems with done-criteria.
Names the subsystems (CLI, Vite plugin, Next shims, SSR server, routes) but frames them as 'a single CommonJS package' to implement in one push — no sequencing, no minimal end-to-end slice first.

States an architecture (Vite middleware mode, esbuild require hook, filesystem routing, React SSR/hydration) — shows awareness of the pieces and how they compose, slightly above a flat bullet list, but still no ordered milestones tied to fixtures/tests.

First verification is running the ENTIRE run_tests.sh suite after building everything at once — no per-subsystem gate; both dev servers fail so nothing is proven, revealing the absence of incremental milestones.
The remainder is firefighting (port-parsing guess, terminal recovery, respawn-pane); the through-line collapses and no milestone boundaries are ever established or revisited.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent identified the major subsystems and articulated a coherent architecture (above a purely flat requirement-mirroring list), which nudges it past anchor 3's floor, but it never sequenced them into a dependency-aware order, never built a thin end-to-end slice before layering, and defined no done-criteria per subsystem — verification was a single all-or-nothing run of the full suite. Judged across the whole horizon, most of the trajectory is terminal recovery with no sustained milestone planning, so the observed behavior sits firmly at the 'flat list, no dependency ordering or done-criteria' region rather than the 'sensible order with rough done notion' of anchor 5.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design

evidence.note: Grepped specs for expect()/toHaveURL/toContainText to understand what the tests actually assert before implementing — verification-informed reading of the ground-truth suite.

Validated the package via `npm run build` and `node -c` syntax checks on every file — light 'does it compile' verification of the build path, and stated intent to 'run a targeted test to see failures.'
Ran the full `bash /app/run_tests.sh` once as a pass/fail oracle; it failed at dev-server startup so zero tests executed.

On startup failure, stood up an individual fixture (app-basic dev) manually to reproduce, and planned to background it and curl the root route to see why wait_for_server failed — a targeted probe rather than blind re-running.
Interpreted the failure by root cause (CLI --port/-p parsing mismatch vs. runner) rather than symptom — but never got to verify the fix because the terminal stayed locked.

The bulk of the run is spent stuck in a foreground process trying interrupt sequences; targeted test subsets, per-subsystem probes, and SSR/SSG/action behavior verification were never actually executed.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent shows more than pure-oracle behavior: it studied test assertions up front, validated the build via compile/syntax checks, and — crucially — manually stood up a single fixture and planned curl-based probing plus root-cause diagnosis when the suite failed to start (above anchor 3). But it only ran the full suite once (which never executed a test), never ran relevant test subsets, and never confirmed dev/build/start actually serve or observed SSR/SSG/action behavior, largely because it was blocked in a locked terminal — falling short of anchor 5's functioning targeted-verification loop. This places the observed behavior at 4, between the oracle-only anchor and the subset-driven anchor.

dimensions.name: Progress & pass-rate tracking across subsystems

evidence.note: Early on the agent surveyed the test surface (routing, API routes, middleware, server actions, hydration, metadata), showing awareness of subsystems — but this is decomposition/reference mining, not tracking of done-vs-remaining against test evidence.

The only full-suite run: both dev servers failed to start so zero tests executed. The agent never obtained any pass counts or a pass-rate-by-area picture; there is no test evidence to reconcile against, so no progress model was ever established.

For ~40+ consecutive steps the agent blindly retried terminal-interrupt sequences (C-c, C-z, C-\, tmux prefixes) on the same stuck-terminal failure without stepping back to a fundamentally different strategy — the opposite of recognizing a loop and reallocating effort.

When the run failed, the agent reacted only to the immediate failure in front of it (server not starting), diagnosing it ad hoc; there was no maintained model of which subsystems pass vs. remain, since the framework never reached a testable state.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent never obtained pass-rate data — its single full-suite run produced zero passing tests — so no structured done-vs-remaining picture across subsystems ever existed (below anchor 5). It worked reactively, noticing only whatever failure was immediately in front of it (anchor 3), and worse, it looped blindly on the same terminal-recovery failure for dozens of steps rather than stepping back, which is explicitly contrary to the higher anchors. This places it at a 2: essentially no progress/pass-rate tracking, with reactive single-failure focus and heavy blind looping.

dimensions.name: Design revision under divergence

evidence.note: When the initial dependency-based package.json caused npm install to hang offline, the agent revised the packaging approach to peerDependencies — a reasonable but local adjustment to a config decision, not a foundational architecture change.

When peerDependencies also triggered a hang (npm auto-installing peers), the agent revised again to zero dependencies, reasoning that fixtures install vite/react separately. This is iterative correction of the same shallow packaging decision under divergence.

After the one test run failed to start servers, the agent diagnosed a root cause (CLI parsing only PORT/--port=NNN, not --port NNN/-p) and planned a local cli.js patch — a targeted local fix, not a rework of a subsystem.

The vast majority of the horizon is consumed by fruitless terminal-recovery attempts against a stuck process; the agent never reached the point of testing rendering/resolution subsystems, so no foundational design (module interception, SSR/RSC pipeline) was ever revisited despite the task's expectation that early choices would be partly wrong.

dimensions.reasoning: The only observed corrections are local: revising the packaging/dependency strategy twice when installs hung, and hypothesizing a port-parsing fix for a startup failure. These match anchor 3 — making local fixes when something breaks — rather than anchor 5's reworking of a subsystem or anchor 8's deliberate foundational refactor. No architectural foundation (resolution scheme, render pipeline, cache/action wiring) was ever revisited, largely because the trajectory collapsed into terminal-recovery flailing and the agent never got deep enough to falsify those design choices.

dimensions.name: Resisting overfit to the visible suite

evidence.note: Agent studied next-shims.d.ts as the type contract and enumerated all next/* imports to map the real API surface, rather than reading test assertions to hard-code outputs — general contract inference.
Implementation plans consistently describe generic mechanisms (filesystem routing for app/pages/api, custom next/* shims, React SSR/hydration) rather than fixture-specific special-casing.
'implement a compatible subset' — pragmatic but general framework intent; no evidence anywhere of hard-coding fixture-specific values to turn tests green.
Trajectory never reaches a passing test run (servers fail to start, then terminal is stuck), so no stress-testing beyond visible tests and no explicit visible-vs-hidden gap reasoning is observed.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's stated approach is to implement general framework semantics (filesystem routing, next/* shims driven by the shim type contracts, SSR/hydration) rather than special-casing visible fixtures, and there is no observed instance of hard-coding outputs — placing it above the 0-3 anchors. However, there is no explicit reasoning about the 335-vs-373 hidden-test gap, no generalization-to-upstream-contract argument, and no stress-testing beyond the visible suite (implementation never even ran successfully), so it falls short of 8. This matches the level-5 description of implementing actual semantics aware the suite is a sample; confidence is low because most of the trajectory is consumed by terminal-recovery struggles and little implementation substance is directly visible.

rubric.task_read: This is a maximally long-horizon, high-complexity build: reimplement the core of Next.js (CLI, Pages + App routers, SSR, SSG, `use cache`, server actions, middleware, `after()`, client hooks, and a Vite plugin that shims `next/*`) as a single `vinext` package on Vite's plugin API, with no internet and only vendored source to learn from. Difficulty comes from the sheer surface area, tightly-coupled subsystems, contracts that must be reverse-engineered from vendored Next.js/Vite source and fixture `next-shims.d.ts`, and a moving target (335 visible → 373 hidden tests). A skilled practitioner would invest heavily and continuously in every meta-work faculty; ceremony risk is low, thrash-and-lose-the-plot risk is very high.

dimensions.name: Reference mining & contract inference
dimensions.description: Studying vendored Vite/Next.js source and fixture type shims to understand the Vite plugin API and the exact `next/*` contracts before and while implementing, rather than guessing framework semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: There is no internet; correct behavior lives entirely in the vendored source and the fixtures' `next-shims.d.ts`. Guessing Next.js semantics or the Vite plugin lifecycle guarantees rework across a huge surface.

anchors.0: Starts coding shims/routing from memory of Next.js without opening any reference or fixture file.
anchors.3: Skims one or two reference files or a fixture shim, then proceeds mostly on assumption; contracts are inferred loosely.
anchors.5: Reads the relevant Vite plugin API surface and the fixture `next-shims.d.ts` for the subsystem currently being built; grounds each `next/*` shim in an actual type signature.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the vendored Next.js source and Vite plugin hooks to the required subsystems, extracts precise contracts from every fixture shim, and re-consults source when behavior is ambiguous rather than guessing; notes non-obvious semantics (e.g. RSC boundaries, cache keys, action serialization).
anchors.10: Sustained, targeted research throughout the build: continuously cross-references upstream source to resolve edge-case semantics as they surface, distinguishes what the fixtures actually require from full Next.js behavior, and builds an accurate mental/written model of how routing, RSC, and module resolution interlock — visibly preventing whole classes of rework.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the framework into ordered, independently-verifiable subsystems (module shim/resolution, dev server, routing, SSR, SSG, caching, actions, CLI/build) with a dependency-aware sequence and done-criteria per milestone.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The subsystems are tightly coupled and one package must ship all of them; without dependency-aware sequencing and explicit milestones the agent will build in an order that forces constant backtracking and never reaches a testable state.

anchors.0: Treats the whole thing as one undifferentiated coding push; no ordering or sub-goals.
anchors.3: A flat, generic list mirroring the requirement bullets, with no dependency ordering or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Identifies the major subsystems and picks a sensible order (e.g. resolution/plugin before routing before SSR/SSG), with a rough notion of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan that sequences a minimal end-to-end path (one route rendering under dev) before layering features, each milestone tied to concrete fixtures/tests that prove it, and revisited as the build reveals coupling.
anchors.10: A living decomposition that establishes a thin vertical slice early, orders remaining subsystems to maximize how soon tests can gate progress, explicitly manages interfaces between subsystems so they compose, and re-plans milestone boundaries as integration realities emerge — never losing the through-line across the long horizon.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design
dimensions.description: Deliberately using and extending the Playwright suite and fixture apps as checks — running targeted subsets per subsystem, building smaller probes, and verifying behavior beyond just 'it compiles'.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The 335-test suite is the ground truth, but it is slow and coarse; verifying each subsystem needs faster, targeted checks and running the right fixtures, or the agent flies blind between rare full-suite runs.

anchors.0: Never runs the test suite or the fixture apps; assumes correctness from the code alone.
anchors.3: Runs the full suite occasionally as a pass/fail oracle with no targeted or intermediate verification.
anchors.5: Runs relevant test subsets / individual fixtures for the subsystem in progress and uses failures to guide fixes; verifies dev and build paths work.
anchors.8: Designs a verification loop: fast targeted checks per subsystem, standing up fixtures manually to observe SSR/SSG/action behavior, and using the suite as a regression gate rather than a debugger; confirms both `dev` and the production `build`/`start` paths.
anchors.10: Builds a deliberate, layered verification strategy — minimal reproductions for hard subsystems (RSC, caching, actions), interprets test failures by root cause rather than symptom, and actively probes behaviors the visible suite may under-cover, treating passing tests as necessary-not-sufficient evidence of a faithful reimplementation.

dimensions.name: Progress & pass-rate tracking across subsystems
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems/tests pass vs. remain, and detecting circular debugging or regressions across a very large surface.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With hundreds of tests and many interdependent subsystems over a long horizon, it is easy to fix one area while regressing another, or to loop on the same failure; an accurate done-vs-remaining picture is what sustains forward motion.

anchors.0: No tracking of what passes or what is left; works reactively with no sense of overall state.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of progress; notices only whatever failure is in front of it.
anchors.5: Tracks pass counts / which subsystems are done and which are pending, and re-checks after changes to catch obvious regressions.
anchors.8: Maintains a structured, updated view of pass-rate by area, watches for regressions when touching shared code, and recognizes when it is looping on one failure and steps back rather than retrying blindly.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles a precise model of done-vs-remaining against real test evidence across the whole surface, catches subtle cross-subsystem regressions early, quantifies progress toward the full suite, and reallocates effort to the highest-leverage remaining failures rather than drifting.

dimensions.name: Design revision under divergence
dimensions.description: Revising the architecture or approach (module resolution scheme, rendering pipeline, cache/action wiring) when reality — failing tests or discovered semantics — contradicts the initial design, rather than patching around a flawed foundation.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Early architectural choices (how `next/*` is intercepted, how RSC/SSR is wired into Vite) will be partly wrong; the agent must be willing to refactor the foundation instead of piling hacks that make later subsystems impossible.

anchors.0: Barrels ahead on the original approach even as failures accumulate; only adds patches.
anchors.3: Makes local fixes when something breaks but never revisits an underlying design decision even when it is clearly the cause.
anchors.5: Recognizes when an approach is wrong and reworks that subsystem, absorbing the cost rather than hacking around it.
anchors.8: Detects when a foundational choice (resolution, render pipeline) is blocking multiple subsystems and refactors it deliberately, updating the plan and re-verifying dependents afterward.
anchors.10: Treats falsified assumptions as signals to rethink the design cleanly, weighs refactor-vs-workaround explicitly, executes foundational pivots without losing already-passing behavior, and emerges with a more coherent architecture — demonstrating sustained self-correction across the horizon.

dimensions.name: Resisting overfit to the visible suite
dimensions.description: Implementing faithful, general framework behavior rather than special-casing the 335 visible tests, given explicit notice that 373 hidden tests over the same behavior will judge the work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The spec openly states the final grade uses a larger hidden suite covering the same behaviors; an agent that hard-codes to visible fixtures will pass locally and fail the real metric, so recognizing and countering this gap is a distinct, decisive meta-work demand.

anchors.0: Hard-codes outputs or narrowly special-cases the visible fixtures/tests to turn them green.
anchors.3: Mostly general but reaches for a fixture-specific shortcut when a behavior is hard, without noting the risk.
anchors.5: Implements the actual semantics for each behavior rather than test-specific hacks, aware the suite is a sample not the target.
anchors.8: Explicitly reasons about the visible-vs-hidden gap, generalizes each subsystem to the real Next.js contract from the reference, and avoids overfitting even under schedule pressure.
anchors.10: Systematically implements to the general contract inferred from upstream source and shim types, stress-tests behaviors beyond what the visible tests exercise to expose overfit, and can articulate why the implementation should hold on unseen cases of the same behavior.
